title: The smaller Pure Land sutra, alone
tomorrow: did he wake up in one night, or over many lives?

cards: Study playlists of rain, waves and birdsong: sounds that ask nothing of you. The smaller Pure Land sutra describes a whole world full of that kind of sound, and then drops in a detail that doesn't fit.
There are birds everywhere, singing day and night. But the same sutra says there are no animals in that land at all. So where did the birds come from?

teach.b: The sutra is short. The Buddha tells his disciple Shariputra about a world far to the west called Sukhavati, the land of bliss, named that because nobody there suffers; there are only joys. Rows of jeweled trees.
Nets of little bells. Lotus pools. Flowers falling from the sky.
And birds, geese, cranes, peacocks, singing all day. Here's the strange part. Their song isn't just pretty.
It's the teaching, sung, and whoever hears it remembers the Buddha, the teaching and the community. Then the Buddha heads off the obvious question.

Shariputra, don't think these birds were born as animals. In that land even the names of the lower worlds don't exist. The birds were made by the Buddha of that land, Amitabha, so the teaching would sound everywhere.
That's the solve: nothing there is just scenery. Even the wind in the bells plays the teaching. Then the practice.

A small root of merit isn't enough to be born there, the sutra says, but whoever hears Amitabha's name and holds it in mind for a night, or up to seven, with an undistracted mind, will see that Buddha at the end.
This is the root of Pure Land Buddhism, where people call the name: the nembutsu in Japan, Namo Amituofo in China, Nam mo A Di Da Phat in Vietnam.

how: Pure Land Buddhists in China, Japan, Korea and Vietnam recite Amitabha's name, aloud or silently, often counting on prayer beads, and the shorter sutra is chanted in Pure Land temples and at funerals.

games.q: what does “the smaller pure land sutra” mean?
o: a guide to building a peaceful garden at a temple
a short sutra on Amitabha's land of bliss and his name
the Buddha's sermon on keeping a household pure

games.q: inside the land of bliss — tap the pairs.
p: the land of bliss, far to the west

s: the birds in the land of bliss were born there as animals
the sutra says even the names of the lower worlds don't exist there; Amitabha made the birds so the teaching would sound everywhere.
the sutra says whoever holds the name in mind for a night, or up to seven, will see Amitabha at the end
with an undistracted mind; this is the root of reciting the name.
the sutra says many good deeds alone will get you born there
it says a small root of merit isn't enough, and points to hearing and holding Amitabha's name.

games.q: a friend says the Pure Land is just a Buddhist vacation garden for good people. using the birds, what's the better reading?
o: even its birds sing the teaching: the land is built to help beings awaken
it's a reward for good people, a peaceful garden to rest in forever
it's poetry about nature, with no teaching in it at all
games.why: the sutra's birds aren't animals; they're the teaching made into song, so that everyone who hears remembers the Buddha, the teaching and the community.

practice: If it's yours to say, say the name softly, Amitabha, once on each out-breath. If not, let the out-breath itself be the sound, and listen to it the way the sutra listens to its birds, as if even this sound could teach.

wordCard.voice: The smaller Pure Land sutra: the short text on Amitabha's land of bliss, where birds sing the teaching and the name is held in mind.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the land of bliss, Amitabha's Buddha-land.

carryVoice: The line for today: the land of bliss, where even the birdsong teaches. Name held.

sources.ref: The smaller Sukhavati-vyuha (the shorter Pure Land sutra; the Amitabha Sutra in Chinese)
